front: Which API field is the canonical signal that an agentic loop should keep iterating vs. terminate?
back: stop_reason. Continue when it equals "tool_use", stop on "end_turn". Never branch on the presence of text content — text and tool_use blocks can coexist in one response.

front: Default topology for multi-agent systems?
back: Hub-and-spoke. A single coordinator delegates to specialist subagents. Avoid arbitrary subagent-to-subagent communication; subagents have no shared memory.

front: Why does a synthesis subagent fail to cite URLs the search subagent retrieved?
back: Subagents do not share context. The coordinator must explicitly include URLs in the synthesis prompt — they don't exist in the synthesis agent's window otherwise.

front: Compliance requirement says all refunds over $250 must notify compliance before being processed. Where do you enforce it?
back: Pre-tool-use hook (deterministic gate). Prompt strengthening is probabilistic and will leak. Keep guidance in prompt, but enforce in code.

front: Three legitimate ways to handle a long conversation that's nearing the context limit?
back: Resume (continue), fork (branch off into a new conversation with summary), or start fresh. Don't silently truncate — summarize explicitly.

front: Symptom: agent ignores a system-prompt rule that's listed alongside 30 others. Fix?
back: Attention dilution. Multi-pass: separate critical rules into a verification step, or move them to a pre-tool gate. Don't pile more rules into the same prompt.

front: Common bug that causes an agent to terminate mid-task in 8% of runs?
back: Treating any text content as completion. Inspect stop_reason instead; text + tool_use can coexist.

front: Role of the coordinator in a hub-and-spoke agent?
back: Owns control flow, routing, and context assembly. Subagents own narrow specialist work. Coordinator decides what to pass and what to keep.

front: Two qualities of a well-designed tool signature?
back: (1) Narrow, single-purpose input — avoid 'do_anything' booleans. (2) Descriptive parameter names + clear description. The LLM is reading these as docs.

front: What problem does the Model Context Protocol (MCP) solve?
back: Standardizes how external tools, resources, and prompts are exposed to LLM clients. Same server works across Claude Desktop, Claude Code, IDE plug-ins, etc.

front: MCP: tool vs. resource?
back: Tool = a callable action with side effects (or computation). Resource = a piece of data the model can read (file, doc, snapshot). Don't model reads as tools when a resource fits.

front: What should a tool return when it can't complete its job?
back: A structured error string the model can reason about — never throw silently. Include the failure category and a remediation hint. The model uses this to decide whether to retry, fall back, or escalate.

front: Symptom: agent picks the wrong tool 30% of the time across a 40-tool catalog. Fix?
back: Reduce tool surface area. Group related calls into a single dispatcher, or split into sub-agents each with a focused toolset. Tool sprawl degrades selection accuracy.

front: Why should tools be idempotent where possible?
back: Agents retry on failure, and the same step may be re-invoked when conversations resume. Idempotent tools make retries safe.

front: Default permission for a destructive tool (delete, deploy, send-money)?
back: Require explicit user approval per call. Don't bake in 'always allow' for irreversible operations.

front: Claude Code: difference between an allowlist and an ask-list?
back: Allowlist: tool runs without confirmation. Ask-list: tool prompts the user before running. Denylist: tool is blocked entirely. Default safe: ask for anything destructive.

front: Purpose of CLAUDE.md?
back: Persistent project instructions Claude reads on every session. Use for repo conventions, build commands, architecture notes, gotchas. Keep it concise — every token is in every prompt.

front: Two main Claude Code hook categories?
back: Pre-tool-use (intercept before a tool runs, can deny) and post-tool-use (react after a tool completes, e.g., auto-format, log). Hooks are deterministic.

front: When should you enable Claude Code's sandbox mode?
back: When letting an agent run untrusted code, scratch experiments, or operations on a workspace you don't want mutated. Sandbox isolates filesystem + network.

front: What is a Claude Code subagent used for?
back: Delegating a focused task with its own scoped toolset, system prompt, and context. Coordinator gets back a summary, not the full transcript — preserves main context.

front: How does Claude Code decide which files to include in context?
back: Mix of: explicit @file mentions, current open editor, recently-edited files, and CLAUDE.md-referenced paths. Be intentional — include too little and it hallucinates; too much and it dilutes.

front: How does Claude Code consume MCP servers?
back: Configure via settings (~/.claude.json or workspace .mcp.json). Each server exposes tools/resources that become callable in any session in that scope.

front: What does Plan mode in Claude Code do?
back: Read-only exploration — Claude can search/read but cannot edit or run side-effectful tools. Used for proposing an approach before committing to changes.

front: Why customize an output style?
back: Match Claude's tone to the audience (terse for engineers, verbose for explanations) and reduce wasted tokens. Useful for agents driving downstream pipelines.

front: Safest default for the Bash tool in a new project?
back: Ask-list for everything; allowlist a small set of read-only commands (ls, cat, git status). Never blanket-allow Bash in unknown repos.

front: Three sections a strong system prompt almost always has?
back: (1) Role + objective. (2) Hard constraints / non-negotiables. (3) Output format / examples. Keep instructions positive ('do X') over negative ('don't Y') where possible.

front: When do few-shot examples beat instructions?
back: When the desired output is structured, idiosyncratic, or hard to describe (formatting, tone, edge-case handling). One concrete example often outperforms a paragraph of rules.

front: When does explicit chain-of-thought help vs. hurt?
back: Helps for multi-step reasoning and verification tasks. Hurts when the user just wants the answer — burns tokens and latency. Use 'think before answering' tags scoped to hard tasks only.

front: What goes at the top of a long prompt to maximize cache hits?
back: Stable content first: long system prompt, knowledge docs, examples. Volatile content last (the user's actual message). Prompt caching only kicks in for repeated prefixes.

front: Why is 'you are an expert X' often weaker than concrete behavior specs?
back: Roleplay is a vibe, not an instruction. 'Cite sources for every claim' or 'reject requests outside X scope' gives the model something to actually enforce.

front: Why does Claude respond well to XML-style tags in prompts?
back: Tags create unambiguous structure — Claude was trained on data where they delimit sections. Use <instructions>, <example>, <user_input> to isolate concerns and reduce instruction-bleed.

front: Reliable way to get strict JSON output?
back: (1) Show the exact schema as an example. (2) Use tool-use forcing if available. (3) Validate + retry on parse failure. Don't rely on 'output valid JSON' as the only instruction.

front: First thing to build before iterating on a prompt?
back: An eval set. Without measurable inputs/outputs you're optimizing on vibes. Even 20 hand-labeled cases beat zero.

front: Two characteristics of a safe retry policy?
back: Exponential backoff with jitter, and a cap on total attempts. Always differentiate retryable (5xx, rate-limit) from non-retryable (4xx) errors.

front: When you hit 429s in production, first move?
back: Respect the Retry-After header. Then look at request shape — are you batching what could be batched, caching what could be cached, parallelizing what should be serial?

front: What is context rot and how do you mitigate it?
back: Long conversations accumulate stale, contradictory, or irrelevant content that degrades responses. Mitigate by periodic summarization, forking, or hard resets at task boundaries.

front: Three signals to log for every agent run?
back: (1) Tool calls with inputs/outputs. (2) stop_reason and token usage. (3) Conversation ID + parent span. Without these, debugging is guesswork.

front: Production eval loop in one line?
back: Sample real traffic → label → measure against held-out set → ship change → re-measure. Repeat. Without this loop, regressions go silent.

front: Where do guardrails belong: in the model prompt or outside the model?
back: Both, but the source of truth is outside. Prompt = soft guidance. Pre/post-tool hooks, input validators, output classifiers = hard enforcement.

front: Strategy when a tool fails partway through a multi-step task?
back: Surface the failure to the model with a structured error so it can reason about recovery. Don't silently retry, don't crash. The agent decides: retry, switch tool, escalate, abort.

front: How to keep token costs predictable at scale?
back: Cache the stable prefix, cap output tokens by task, sample expensive paths, and measure cost-per-task as a first-class metric — not just latency.

front: Defense-in-depth against prompt injection?
back: Isolate untrusted content in tags, treat all tool outputs as untrusted by default, apply allowlists/denylists on actions the agent can take after consuming external content, and log everything.

front: Safe rollout pattern for a prompt or model change?
back: Canary on a small traffic slice with the eval set running in shadow. Watch quality + cost + latency. Promote only when all three hold.
